title: In Praise of Boredom
paragraphs: There was a time, not so long ago, when waiting meant doing nothing. Passengers at a bus stop in Santiago would stare at the road, count the cars or simply think. Seldom did anyone reach for a device, because there was no device to reach for. Today, hardly has a queue formed before every head bows towards a glowing screen. We have, it seems, declared war on empty time, and we are winning it so thoroughly that we have forgotten what we were fighting for.

What troubles me is not the screens themselves but the reflex behind them. Boredom is an uncomfortable signal, rather like hunger, and we have learned to silence it the instant it appears. Yet discomfort is not always a fault to be repaired. Researchers who study creativity have long suggested that idle stretches allow the mind to wander, to connect ideas that would otherwise stay apart. Whether that explanation is complete remains debated, but the pattern matches ordinary experience: the best idea of the week rarely arrives at a desk.

A friend of mine, a translator in Lima, admits that her best solutions come while she is washing dishes. Were she to listen to a podcast during that time, she says, the solutions would vanish. She is not claiming that every idle moment produces genius; most produce nothing at all. Her point is subtler: only by tolerating the nothing can one reach the something. It is a bargain few of us are willing to make, since the nothing is certain and the something is not.

Critics will object that boredom is a luxury of the comfortable. A night-shift cleaner on a long bus ride home, they say, does not need advice to embrace emptiness; she needs rest, or entertainment, or both. They are right, and I do not wish to romanticise tiredness. Nevertheless, the argument cuts both ways. If time is scarce for many people, then handing what remains to applications designed to hold attention is hardly a generous act. Our empty minutes are among the few things we still own.

There is also the matter of what we teach the young. Children who are never left alone with their thoughts may grow up believing that silence is a malfunction. I remember long afternoons at my grandmother's house in Valparaíso, when there was nothing to do but watch the light move across the wall. Those afternoons felt endless then. In memory, they feel like the place where my imagination first learned to move.

Nor should we imagine that the solution is heroic abstinence. Throwing one's phone into a lake would solve little and cost a great deal. A more modest experiment is enough: leave the device in a pocket during one short wait each day, and watch what the mind does when nobody is directing it. At first it will complain loudly. After a week, it may start to offer something more interesting than a complaint.

I do not pretend that boredom is pleasant; it was never meant to be. But it is the soil in which attention grows, and no gardener praises soil for being comfortable. Perhaps what we need is not another tool for filling the gaps in our day, but the courage to leave some of them open. Should we manage that, we might find that the empty hours were never empty at all.

questions.q: The author believes that empty moments can help the mind connect ideas.
questions.explain_es: El texto dice que los momentos ociosos permiten 'to connect ideas that would otherwise stay apart'.

questions.q: The author recommends that readers give up their phones completely.
questions.explain_es: Dice que tirar el teléfono a un lago 'would solve little' y propone solo un experimento modesto: dejarlo en el bolsillo durante una espera breve.

questions.q: What can we infer about the author's reaction to the critics' objection?
options: He thinks it deserves no reply at all
He dismisses it as entirely mistaken
He accepts it but finds it incomplete
questions.explain_es: Inferencia: 'They are right' muestra acuerdo parcial, pero 'the argument cuts both ways' indica que la objeción no basta.

options: Reflective and gently persuasive
Detached and strictly scientific
Angry and openly accusatory
questions.explain_es: Tono: el autor reflexiona, admite dudas ('Whether that explanation is complete remains debated') y persuade con suavidad, sin acusar.

questions.q: Why does the author mention the translator in Lima?
options: To give a concrete example of his idea
To prove that boredom produces genius
To show that podcasts improve translation
questions.explain_es: Propósito: la traductora ilustra con un caso real la idea de que hay que tolerar 'the nothing' para llegar a 'the something'. Ella misma aclara que no todo momento ocioso produce genio.

questions.q: How does the fourth paragraph relate to the argument?
options: It introduces a new and unrelated topic
It raises an objection and then answers it
It repeats the opening anecdote in detail
questions.explain_es: Estructura: el párrafo plantea la objeción ('Critics will object...') y la responde con 'the argument cuts both ways'.

options: badly used
hard to find
freely given
questions.explain_es: 'Scarce' significa escaso: hay poco tiempo disponible, por eso el autor habla de 'what remains'.

title: The City That Never Stops Talking
paragraphs: Every morning at ten to six, a car alarm in my street in São Paulo performs its solo. By half past, the bakery's delivery van has joined in, followed by a neighbour's drill and, somewhere above them all, a helicopter. Having lived here for eleven years, I like to think I have grown used to it. My body, however, keeps a different record: I wake tired, I read tired and I lose my temper over small things.

It would be easy to dismiss this as the price of living in a big city, and for a long time I did. Yet the evidence is hard to ignore. The World Health Organization has linked long-term exposure to traffic noise with disturbed sleep and a higher risk of heart disease. Noise is not merely an irritation; it is a public health problem that happens to be invisible. Unlike smog, it leaves no stain on the buildings, and that may explain why politicians rarely mention it.

What bothers me most is how unevenly the burden is shared. Residents of the wealthy districts pay for double glazing and quiet courtyards, while families living beside the main avenues, often renting rooms for a few hundred reais a month, have no such protection. Quiet, in other words, has become a commodity. Those who can afford it sleep well; those who cannot are told to be grateful for the opportunities that city life brings.

Some will say that a city without noise would be a city without life, and I sympathise. The calls of street vendors, the football on a radio, the music from a passing wedding: these are part of what makes a place feel inhabited. But that is a defence of sound, not of noise. The difference lies in choice. A sound we can walk towards or away from is a pleasure; a sound that follows us through the walls is a trespass.

I should add that nobody expects silence. A city is a machine for gathering people, and people make noise; that is part of the bargain. What we can reasonably expect is a limit, in the same way that we expect limits on the smoke from factory chimneys or the waste poured into rivers. Nobody calls those limits an attack on industry, and the comparison is worth keeping in mind.

Several cities have shown that change is possible. Better road surfaces, lower speed limits at night and stricter rules for building sites have reduced noise without making streets feel dead. None of these measures is expensive compared with the cost of treating the illnesses that noise helps to cause. What is missing is not money but attention, and attention is something citizens can demand.

So I have started a small campaign of my own. Armed with a cheap sound meter and a notebook, I record the worst hours in my street and send the results to the district council every month. I do not expect a quick reply. Still, a problem that has been measured is harder to deny than one that has only been complained about, and I intend to keep measuring until somebody listens.
glossary: bien que se compra y se vende, mercancía

title: The Ghost Tenants
paragraphs: When Daniela Quispe moved to a new flat in Arequipa last spring, she paid a deposit of 2,400 soles to a landlord she had only met on a rental website. The keys never arrived. The man whose photograph appeared on the listing, it later emerged, did not exist, and the flat belonged to a family who had never advertised it. Ms Quispe is one of at least forty tenants who, according to complaints reviewed for this investigation, lost money in similar circumstances over the past year.

The scheme works because it is simple. A fraudster copies photographs from genuine advertisements, lowers the rent slightly and asks interested tenants to pay a deposit before visiting. Pressure is applied through claims that other applicants are waiting. By the time the victim realises something is wrong, the account that received the transfer has been emptied and the profile deleted. Several tenants told us they had ignored their own doubts precisely because the price seemed fair.

The platform on which most of the advertisements appeared says it removes suspicious listings quickly. Our review suggests otherwise. Of the twenty-three fraudulent advertisements we tracked, eleven remained visible for more than a week after being reported. A spokesperson, who declined to be named, said the company relied on users to flag problems and was investing in automatic detection. No timetable for that investment was offered.

The consequences extend beyond lost money. Two of the tenants interviewed were students who had travelled from other provinces and found themselves without a place to sleep on the day lessons began. One was allowed to stay on a friend's floor for three weeks. Another had to drop out of the semester altogether. Such stories rarely appear in official statistics, which count the fraud but not what follows from it.

Police officers told us that the cases are difficult to pursue. The accounts used are frequently opened with false documents, and the money is moved within hours. Moreover, victims often wait several days before filing a report, partly out of embarrassment. A consumer-rights lawyer in Lima argued that the burden should shift: platforms, he said, are the only party able to verify identities at scale, and they profit from every listing.

One local official, whom we reached by telephone, said that the council had received only a handful of formal complaints and therefore saw no reason to act. That reasoning is circular. Victims who have lost their savings are rarely in the mood to spend days filling in forms, and several told us they had assumed that nothing would come of it. A low number of reports is not proof of a small problem; it may be proof of a discouraging process.

There are practical precautions. Tenants can request a video call from inside the property, search for the photographs online and refuse to transfer money before signing a contract. None of this should be necessary, of course. Until platforms accept responsibility for the listings they sell, the advice remains the same as ever: if an offer looks too good to be true, it probably is. The difficulty is that, when you are desperate for a home, the offer rarely looks suspicious enough.

title: The Cover Version Problem
paragraphs: Few things divide music lovers as reliably as the cover version. For some listeners, a song belongs to the voice that first recorded it, and any later attempt is a kind of impertinence. For others, a good song is a house that anyone may move into, redecorate and make their own. It is the second view that I wish to defend here, although not without reservations.

History offers plenty of evidence for the defence. Many of the pieces that people consider definitive were in fact recorded by somebody else first. What turns a cover into a classic is rarely fidelity; it is the willingness to take a risk. A singer who copies the original note for note gives us an imitation, which is a respectable thing but also a dispensable one. A singer who finds a hidden meaning in the same words gives us a conversation across decades.

Consider the tradition of Latin American boleros, which travelled from Cuba to Mexico to Argentina and changed accent at every port. A song written in Havana acquired a different weight when sung by a Mexican trio, and a different one again when a young singer in Buenos Aires slowed it down by half. Nobody in that chain was cheating. They were doing what folk music has always done: borrowing, bending and passing on.

The trouble begins when the market gets involved. Streaming platforms reward recognition, and a familiar tune with a new voice is a safe investment. Hence the flood of acoustic versions, slowed-down remixes and nostalgic reworkings that sound as though they were produced by a formula. What worries me is not that these exist but that they crowd out the unfamiliar. A playlist made entirely of reinterpretations is a museum that never acquires anything new.

Nor is the problem confined to pop. In recent years, orchestras have rearranged video-game soundtracks, jazz musicians have taken on rock anthems, and cumbia bands have recorded whole albums of songs first made famous in other countries. The best of these projects do not feel like marketing. They feel like curiosity, and curiosity, unlike nostalgia, usually points forward.

There is also a question of fairness. Songwriters whose work is covered earn royalties, but those who have never been covered earn nothing, and the gap between the two groups is widening. If one wishes to support originality, one could do worse than to buy a ticket for an unknown band's concert rather than stream another version of a famous ballad.

In the end, my position is a modest one. Covers are not a threat to creativity; indifference is. Let a thousand singers reinterpret an old song, provided that somebody, somewhere, is still writing a new one. The measure of a musical culture is not how well it remembers its classics, but how generously it makes room for the songs that have not been written yet.
glossary: versión (de una canción ya grabada por otro artista)

questions.q: The author argues that exact imitation is what makes a cover memorable.
questions.explain_es: Afirma que lo que convierte una versión en clásico 'is rarely fidelity; it is the willingness to take a risk'.

To criticise Mexican musicians

title: How Bees Make Sense of Numbers
paragraphs: A honeybee's brain contains only about a million neurons, a tiny fraction of the number in a human head. It is therefore surprising that researchers have repeatedly found it capable of tasks once thought to require far larger brains. Among the most intriguing is the apparent ability to deal with quantities, a skill that used to be considered uniquely human, or at least uniquely vertebrate.

In experiments that have been repeated in several laboratories, bees are trained to fly into a tunnel and choose between two panels, each showing a different number of shapes. A drop of sugar water rewards the correct choice; a bitter liquid punishes the wrong one. After enough trials, bees learn to select the panel with, say, three shapes rather than two, even when the shapes are new and arranged differently. The insects, it seems, are not simply memorising a picture.

Some studies go further. It has been reported that bees can grasp that nothing is fewer than something, a concept that children usually take years to understand. Other work suggests that they can perform very simple addition and subtraction, provided the numbers are small. These claims have been debated, and some researchers argue that bees may be using shortcuts, such as estimating total area, rather than counting in the strict sense. The disagreement is healthy; it forces scientists to design cleverer tests.

Why would a bee need numbers at all? One plausible answer lies in foraging. A worker who can compare the number of flowers in two patches, or remember how many landmarks she has passed on the way home, saves time and energy. Over many generations, a small advantage of this kind can be decisive. In evolutionary terms, arithmetic need not be a luxury; it may be a by-product of efficient navigation.

Another line of research looks at how bees learn from one another. In one study, bumblebees that had watched a trained companion pull a string to reach a sugary reward later learned to do the same, even though nothing in nature resembles that task. This kind of social learning had been thought rare among insects. It adds to a growing picture of animals whose minds are more flexible than their size would lead us to expect.

The findings also raise a modest but interesting question about how brains work. If complex behaviour can arise from so few neurons, then perhaps size matters less than organisation. Computer scientists have taken note: models inspired by insect brains are already being tested to control small robots, which must make decisions with very limited processing power.

None of this means that bees understand mathematics as we do. Counting a handful of objects is a world away from proving a theorem. Nevertheless, the research invites a certain humility. Each time we assume that a skill belongs only to us, an animal comes along and shows us otherwise, and often it is an animal small enough to land on a teaspoon.

questions.q: In the experiments, bees were rewarded with sugar water for choosing the correct panel.
questions.explain_es: El texto dice: 'A drop of sugar water rewards the correct choice'.

questions.q: All researchers agree that bees count in the strict sense of the word.
questions.explain_es: Algunos argumentan que las abejas 'may be using shortcuts, such as estimating total area, rather than counting'.

options: Impatient with the researchers involved
Positive about its effect on research
Worried that it slows progress

options: To suggest a reason why numerical skills could evolve
To prove that bees are cleverer than other insects
To describe how bees communicate with each other

curiosity

title: The Cartographer of Unmapped Streets
paragraphs: On a hillside above Guadalajara, where the paved road gives way to steps and then to a dirt path, Camila Ortega stops to check her phone. The screen shows a blank space. According to the official map, no street exists here, yet she has just walked past a bakery, a school and nineteen houses. 'Blank spaces are not empty,' she says. 'They are places that somebody has decided not to count.'

Ortega, forty-one, trained as a geographer but spent her twenties working in an insurance office, drawing risk maps for neighbourhoods she never visited. The turning point came when a flood damaged a settlement that the company's data classified as uninhabited. 'Three hundred families were living in a place that did not exist on paper,' she recalls. 'Nobody could claim help for them, because nobody could prove they were there.'

She left her job and founded a small organisation that trains residents to map their own streets. Armed with secondhand phones and free software, volunteers record house numbers, water taps, pharmacies and the shortcuts that children use to reach school. The data is then published openly, so that ambulances, delivery drivers and local authorities can use it. In six years, the group has charted more than forty districts across three states.

Not everyone has welcomed the work. Some residents worry that visibility will bring higher taxes or eviction, and a few landowners have objected strongly. Ortega takes these fears seriously. Before any mapping begins, the volunteers hold open meetings, and a street is only recorded if the people who live on it agree. 'A map is a form of power,' she says, 'and power should not arrive uninvited.'

The results are modest but tangible. In one neighbourhood, an ambulance that had previously taken twenty-five minutes to find a patient arrived in nine. In another, a local council, presented with detailed data, finally agreed to install street lighting. Such victories do not make headlines, but they change the daily routine of those concerned.

The work is physically demanding. On a typical Saturday, Ortega and a dozen volunteers, most of them students or retired teachers, start at seven in the morning and climb for six hours, stopping to talk with anyone who opens a door. They carry no uniforms and no official badges, only water bottles and a laminated card that explains, in simple language, what the project is and what it will do with the information.

Ortega is frank about the limits of her approach. Maps do not build sewers or pay wages, and she is wary of people who treat technology as a cure. What she offers, she insists, is merely a first step: a way for a community to be seen. As she walks down the hill, she adds a last point to the screen, a small green dot where a woman is selling fruit. 'There,' she says. 'Now it exists.'

questions.q: Camila Ortega worked in an insurance company before she founded her organisation.
questions.explain_es: El texto dice que pasó su veintena en una oficina de seguros, 'drawing risk maps'.

As an idealist who ignores real problems
As a thoughtful person aware of her limits

options: To teach readers how to use mapping software

options: a medicine
a complete solution

title: The Last Ferry to Isla Grande
focus: Narrative tenses, inversion and participle clauses
paragraphs: The ferry left the mainland at dusk, as it had every evening of Tomás Ibarra's childhood. He stood at the rail, a suitcase between his feet, watching the lights of the port shrink behind him. Never had he expected to make this crossing again. Twenty years earlier, he had promised himself that the island would be something he had survived, not something he would return to.

His mother's letter had been short. The house needed a decision, she wrote, and she could not make it alone. Tomás had read it three times in his flat in Madrid, searching for a hint of reproach, and found none. That was precisely what disturbed him. The woman he remembered would have complained for two pages about his silence; this one simply asked for help.

On the deck, an old man was selling coffee from a flask. 'You're Ibarra's boy,' he said, without asking. Tomás nodded, surprised that anyone remembered. 'Your father mended my nets once, and never charged me.' The man poured a cup and refused the coins that were offered. 'Pay me when you leave,' he said, and laughed as though he had told a good joke.

The island appeared slowly, a long shadow rising from the water. Lanterns flickered along the quay, fewer than he remembered. When the boat touched the dock, Tomás saw a small figure waiting at the end of it, wrapped in a grey shawl. She did not wave. She simply watched him come, hands folded, as one might watch weather approaching.

'You've grown thin,' she said finally, taking the suitcase from his hand before he could prevent her. It was not what he had prepared himself to hear. For weeks he had rehearsed speeches in the shower, on the train, in the queue at the airport: explanations, apologies, small defences of the life he had built. None of them seemed necessary now, and he felt oddly disarmed, like a soldier arriving at a battle that had ended years ago.

They walked home in silence. The house was smaller than in his memory, its paint peeling, its garden gone to weeds. Inside, however, nothing had been moved. His father's boots still stood by the door, and the clock above the stove still ran five minutes fast, because nobody had dared to correct it. 'I don't want to sell,' his mother said at last, 'but I don't want you to think you have to stay.'

He understood then that the letter had not been a request for help but an offer of freedom, wrapped in the only language she had. Tomás set his suitcase down beside the boots. Outside, the ferry sounded its horn and turned back towards the mainland, and for the first time in twenty years he did not feel that he was missing it.

questions.q: Tomás's mother complained at length about his silence in her letter.
questions.explain_es: La carta fue corta y Tomás no encontró 'a hint of reproach'; eso es lo que lo inquieta.

questions.q: The old man on the ferry knew who Tomás was without being told.
questions.explain_es: El hombre dice 'You're Ibarra's boy' 'without asking'.

questions.q: What does the clock above the stove suggest about the house?
options: It was a gift from the old man
The family could not afford to repair it
The mother wanted to preserve things as they were
questions.explain_es: Inferencia: sigue adelantado cinco minutos 'because nobody had dared to correct it'; la familia conservó todo tal como estaba.

questions.q: What is the mood of the story's ending?
options: Quiet and gently resolved
Playful and lightly humorous
Tense and full of anger
questions.explain_es: Tono: el final es sereno; Tomás deja la maleta y 'did not feel that he was missing' el ferri.

questions.q: Why does the author describe the mother as watching him 'as one might watch weather approaching'?
options: To explain that a storm is coming
To suggest she is not pleased to see him
To show she is calm but guarded
questions.explain_es: Propósito de la imagen: ella no saluda y observa con las manos cruzadas; la comparación transmite una calma reservada, no hostilidad.

questions.q: How does the final paragraph change the way we read the first one?
options: It shows the mother's request was really a gift
It proves the island was never important
It reveals that Tomás will sell the house
questions.explain_es: Estructura: la carta que parecía pedir ayuda era 'an offer of freedom'; el regreso que él temía se transforma en reconciliación.

questions.q: In 'searching for a hint of reproach', 'hint' means…
options: a strong warning
a slight sign
a clear order
questions.explain_es: 'Hint' es una pista o indicio leve: Tomás busca una señal de reproche en la carta y no la encuentra.

title: Municipal Water Audit: Executive Summary
paragraphs: ## 1. Purpose and scope

This summary presents the principal findings of an independent audit of the municipal water supply in San Isidro del Valle, a town of approximately 85,000 inhabitants. The audit, commissioned by the town council, covered the period from January to December of last year and examined water losses, billing accuracy and maintenance practices. It was not designed to assess the quality of drinking water, which is monitored separately.
## 2. Main findings

Of every hundred litres of treated water entering the network, an estimated thirty-eight never reach a paying customer. Roughly two thirds of this loss is attributable to leaking pipes, many of which were laid more than fifty years ago. The remainder results from illegal connections, faulty meters and unmetered public use. The leakage rate is high but not exceptional for towns of comparable size in the region.

Billing practices represent a second area of concern. Approximately one in five household meters was found to be unreadable or out of service, with the consequence that charges for those properties were estimated rather than measured. Several households were consequently overcharged, while others paid far less than their actual consumption warranted. No evidence of deliberate manipulation was found.

Losses are not evenly distributed. The three oldest districts, which together account for roughly a quarter of all connections, generate more than half of the total leakage. By contrast, the neighbourhoods built in the last fifteen years record losses below the regional average. This pattern suggests that age of infrastructure, rather than poor management alone, is the decisive factor, although the two are clearly related.
## 3. Maintenance and investment

The utility's maintenance budget has remained virtually unchanged for six years in spite of rising costs. Most repairs are carried out after a pipe has burst, rather than as part of a planned programme. This reactive approach is more expensive in the long term, since emergency work costs considerably more than scheduled replacement and interrupts supply to residents. Staff interviewed during the audit also reported shortages of spare parts and vehicles, which delay repairs by several days on average. Residents in affected streets, in turn, are often left without service for most of a working day, with little advance notice.
## 4. Recommendations

The audit team recommends that the council prioritise the replacement of the oldest sections of the network, beginning with the three districts where leakage is highest. It further recommends the installation of new meters in all households within two years, and the introduction of a public dashboard showing monthly losses. Together, these measures could reduce losses by an estimated ten percentage points within five years.

It should be noted that the figures above are estimates, and that the margin of error is greater in districts where meters are missing. The team therefore advises that the audit be repeated after two years, so that progress can be measured against a more reliable baseline.
glossary: reactivo, que responde cuando el problema ya ocurrió
punto de referencia, base de comparación

questions.q: The audit evaluated the quality of the town's drinking water.
questions.explain_es: El informe dice que 'It was not designed to assess the quality of drinking water'.

questions.q: According to the report, most of the water loss is caused by leaking pipes.
questions.explain_es: Afirma que 'Roughly two thirds of this loss is attributable to leaking pipes'.

questions.q: What can be inferred about the town's repair policy?
options: It follows a carefully scheduled programme
It spends more than it needs to on fixing problems
It spends too much on new meters
questions.explain_es: Inferencia: se repara tras la rotura, y esto 'is more expensive in the long term' que el reemplazo programado.

questions.q: What is the tone of the report?
options: Casual and humorous
Emotional and openly critical
Formal and carefully cautious
questions.explain_es: Tono: usa lenguaje formal y matizado ('No evidence of deliberate manipulation was found', 'figures are estimates').

questions.q: Why does the report include a final note about estimates?
options: To ask the council for more funding
To suggest that the audit was a failure
To warn the reader about the limits of the data
questions.explain_es: Propósito: advierte que las cifras son estimaciones, con mayor margen de error donde faltan medidores, y por eso recomienda repetir la auditoría.

questions.q: How is the report organised?
options: By the date on which each problem was found
By purpose, findings, maintenance and recommendations
By the names of the districts audited
questions.explain_es: Estructura: las secciones numeradas siguen el esquema habitual de un informe: propósito, hallazgos, mantenimiento y recomendaciones.

questions.q: In 'Billing practices represent a second area of concern', 'concern' means…
options: a kind of celebration
a business company
a source of worry
questions.explain_es: 'Concern' aquí es motivo de preocupación; los problemas de facturación son un segundo punto problemático.

title: The Right to Be Forgotten
paragraphs: For most of human history, forgetting was automatic. A foolish remark made at a party, a failed business or an embarrassing photograph would fade as people moved on, and few outside one's circle would ever hear of it. The internet has changed that arrangement. Information that once vanished now persists, and a search engine can retrieve a teenager's worst afternoon decades after the teenager has become somebody else.

In 2014, the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled in a case brought by a Spanish citizen that, under certain conditions, individuals may ask search engines to remove links to outdated or irrelevant information about them. The decision became known as the right to be forgotten, a phrase that is slightly misleading. Nothing is erased from the original website; only the link in the search results disappears. The information remains, but it becomes harder to find.

Supporters of the ruling stress human dignity. A person who was acquitted of a crime, or who declared bankruptcy fifteen years ago, should not be defined for ever by a single headline. Had the same story appeared in a printed newspaper, it would by now gather dust in an archive. Why, they ask, should the digital version be treated differently simply because it is easier to find?

Opponents reply, with equal conviction, that the public has a legitimate interest in knowing the past. A politician with a record of corruption, a doctor who was suspended or a company that polluted a river may all prefer to be forgotten, but the rest of us have good reasons to remember. If every embarrassing fact could be removed on request, powerful people would be the first to apply, since they are the ones with lawyers.

The difficulty, then, lies in drawing a line, and no formula will draw it perfectly. Courts must weigh the nature of the information, the role the person plays in public life and the time that has passed. A minor offence committed at nineteen is not the same as a fraud committed by a minister, and a rule that treats them alike would be unjust in one direction or the other.

It is also worth remembering that the debate is not the same everywhere. Legal traditions differ on how to balance privacy against freedom of expression, and what counts as acceptable in one country may be unthinkable in another. A single global standard seems unlikely, which means that the same search may give different results depending on where it is made, an outcome that satisfies nobody completely.

Perhaps the deeper issue is that societies have not yet agreed on how long a mistake should follow somebody. We have always granted a kind of social forgiveness, however imperfect. Whether technology should be allowed to remove it, or whether law should step in to restore it, is a question that is likely to occupy us for many years. What seems clear is that, if we are to live with permanent memory, we shall need to become more forgiving ourselves.

questions.q: According to the text, the 2014 ruling deletes information from the original website.
questions.explain_es: Dice que 'Nothing is erased from the original website; only the link in the search results disappears'.

questions.q: The author says that powerful people could take advantage of a rule with no limits.
questions.explain_es: Indica que, si todo se pudiera eliminar a petición, 'powerful people would be the first to apply, since they are the ones with lawyers'.

questions.q: What can we infer about the author's view of the debate?
options: He supports the opponents of the ruling
He believes each case needs careful judgement
He thinks the problem has an easy answer
questions.explain_es: Inferencia: afirma que 'no formula will draw it perfectly' y que los tribunales deben sopesar cada caso; no se decanta por un bando.

questions.q: How does the author treat the two opposing positions?
options: He presents both with fairness
He ridicules the supporters
He ignores the opponents
questions.explain_es: Actitud/tono: expone con igual detalle los argumentos de partidarios y detractores ('with equal conviction').

questions.q: Why does the author refer to a printed newspaper?
options: To compare how old stories were once forgotten
To suggest that printed articles are unreliable
To show that newspapers are better than websites
questions.explain_es: Propósito: el periódico impreso acabaría 'gathering dust in an archive'; sirve para contrastar el olvido natural del pasado con la persistencia digital.

questions.q: What is the function of the fifth paragraph?
options: It repeats the arguments of the opponents
It tells a personal story about the author
It identifies the main difficulty of the issue
questions.explain_es: Estructura: tras presentar ambas posturas, el párrafo señala la dificultad: 'The difficulty, then, lies in drawing a line'.

questions.q: In 'a phrase that is slightly misleading', 'misleading' means…
options: extremely well known
giving a wrong impression
too long to remember
questions.explain_es: 'Misleading' es engañoso: la frase sugiere que todo se borra, cuando solo desaparece el enlace.
